reasoning:
There was no previous guidance, so this is the first slow update. The skill body did not change in effect between epochs: 0 improvements, 0 regressions, 12 stable successes and 8 persistent failures. The 12 successes (Buffalo, The Stand, Thomas Hardy, Emperor, bleat, Apogee and others) are clean, well-supported entities where Rules 2-4 already work, so the guidance must not disturb them.

The 8 persistent failures fall into a few systemic patterns that the existing rules did not fix:
1. Wrong answer type, answering an anchor or related entity. 'this English circumnavigator' got 'San Francisco', a place named in the clue. 'She played Tina Turner...' got the film title instead of the actress (Angela Bassett). 'Its area equals pi r squared' got 'Area' and then 'radius', words from the clue, instead of Circle. Rule 2 already says this, but the model is not applying it, so it needs an explicit pre-answer type check.
2. Misreading the factual direction or ignoring the clue's own hint. 'Admitted to U.N. in 1971' got Taiwan, which was expelled; the answer is China. 'Head of the former head of the country, seen here:(U.S. president, '81-'89)' got 'Starr'. The parenthetical caption of the image or audio clue states who the answer is (Ronald Reagan), and the model ignored it for noisy passages.
3. Over-long or mis-formed names. 'Athens Classic Marathon' was given even though Rule 4 uses this exact case as its example ('the marathon'), so the instruction was not salient enough. 'Francis Drake' lost to '(Sir Francis) Drake', so for a knight the 'Sir' form or the bare surname is safer.
4. Inflection mismatch. 'This term for following a winding & turning course' wanted the gerund 'Meandering', and the model gave 'meander'.

The new guidance therefore adds a short mandatory pre-answer checklist (type check, no clue words, caption and colon-format handling, sanity-check the fact with own knowledge, form matching). It restates the marathon-style trimming forcefully, adds the Sir and gerund points, and explicitly protects the verbatim-archive and short-core-answer behaviors that produce the stable successes.
slow_update_content:
## Strategic guidance (read before every answer)

The failures that keep recurring are not knowledge gaps. They are TYPE errors, ignored hints, and form errors. Run this checklist silently on every clue before writing the answer tags. Keep the behaviors that already work: copy verbatim archive answers (Rule 3), and give the bare short core answer.

### 1. Type-check the slot FIRST
- Pronoun or noun in the clue -> required answer type. 'She/He/Who/this man/this woman/this English circumnavigator/this playwright' -> a PERSON'S NAME. Never answer with a film, song, ship, book or place, even if the passages are full of that title. 'She played Tina Turner on the big screen & Rosa Parks on TV' -> the actress (Angela Bassett), NOT the film 'What's Love Got to Do with It'.
- 'Its area equals pi r squared', 'its sides...', 'its capital is...' -> name the THING that owns the property (Circle). Never answer with the property or a variable already in the clue (Area, radius).
- Any proper noun or content word already in the clue (San Francisco, Golden Hind, Panathenaic) is an anchor, never the answer. If your candidate appears in the clue text, reject it and ask 'what thing is the clue describing?' ('English circumnavigator who put the Golden Hind in for repairs' -> Sir Francis Drake).

### 2. Captions, parentheticals and colon formats are the clue's key
- Many clues are from picture or audio rounds: 'seen here', 'heard here', or a trailing parenthetical like '(U.S. president, '81-'89)' or '("Papillon Barbie")'. The parenthetical is the caption and usually tells you exactly who or what the answer is. Use it with your own knowledge: 'U.S. president, '81-'89' -> Ronald Reagan. Do NOT pick a random surname from noisy passages (e.g., 'Starr'). The answer must satisfy the caption's role and dates.
- 'CATEGORY:clue' with a colon, e.g. 'A knighted Englishman:The Golden Hind': the part before the colon describes the answer and the part after is the item linked to it. Answer the person or thing that fits both halves (Sir Francis Drake).

### 3. Sanity-check facts with your own knowledge; read the verb
- When the passages are generic, off-topic or contradictory, trust well-established knowledge over a stray passage. Check the direction of the event: 'finally ADMITTED to the U.N. in 1971' -> the People's Republic of China (answer: China), not Taiwan, which lost its seat that year. 'Asia's population giant' means China (or India only if the date and event fit).
- Make sure your answer fits every detail (year, role, action), not just the topic.

### 4. Final-form rules that keep costing exact matches
- GENERIC EVENT / THING: when the clue says 'this' + a generic thing (a race, festival, war, event) and the passages give a long proper name with a city, sponsor or year, answer with the generic name only. 'the finish of this, won by Spiridon Louis' -> 'the marathon' / 'Marathon', NOT 'Athens Classic Marathon'. If your answer is 3 or more words, ask whether a shorter standard name exists and use it.
- KNIGHTS: for a person the clue calls 'knighted' or 'Sir', or who is conventionally known with the title (Sir Francis Drake, Sir Walter Raleigh, Sir Isaac Newton), answer in the full titled form 'Sir Firstname Lastname'. Plain 'Francis Drake' lost to the key '(Sir Francis) Drake'. Do not add 'Sir' to people who are not knights (Thomas Hardy and Dwight D. Eisenhower were right as written).
- GRAMMATICAL FORM: match the form of the clue's definition. 'This term for FOLLOWING a winding & turning course' -> the -ing form 'Meandering', not 'meander'. A definition starting with 'to ...' or a verb phrase wants the verb form that fits ('to move in a winding course' -> 'meander'). A definition describing a noun gets a noun ('It's the cry of a sheep' -> 'bleat'). Pick the inflection that substitutes grammatically into the clue's phrase.

### 5. Never give a non-answer
Always commit to one specific entity. If the passages are useless, answer from your own knowledge using the type check above. Never answer with a clue word or a guess of the wrong type.
